the implications of the emergence of a new apparel export destination, South Africa, on Lesotho's industrial upgrading and development.
the question of how the apparel industry in a low income country can be upgraded in order to become more sustainable.
the question of how the integration of developing country apparel producers into global value chains can contribute to their development.

the South African market is more conducive for functional and product upgrading, local linkage development, and skill development in Lesothon's apparel industry.
the South African market is more beneficial to Lesotho than the US market, in terms of upgrading and industrial development.
the South African value chain has a higher potential for upgrading, local linkage development, and skill development than the Taiwanese chain.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
Lesotho has achieved significant functional upgrading in both markets.
while the Taiwanese value chain variant has been instrumental in Lesotho achieving its export growth, its impact on industrial upgrading and development is limited.
the apparel industry in Lesotho has been successful in terms of functional and product upgrading, but has not been successful in terms and scale of local linkages and skill development.
The main takeaway from our work is that
apparel value chains are not a homogeneous entity and that their characteristics matter for upgrading and development.

the South African market has the potential to be a more effective driver of upgrading in Lesotho because it is more embedded in the local economy, and thus provides greater opportunities for local suppliers to upgrade their capabilities and enter higher value activities in the apparel value chain.
the upgrading potential of the apparel industry in developing countries is highly dependent on the type of value chain variant in which they are integrated.
